_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla, right on the sked. First lesson tonight, and it starts with the two questions every June brings: will the morning grey burn off, and do the white puffs that come up by mid-morning mean rain?

replies.back: Work through the lesson and tell me. Once you know what a cloud is made of, both questions answer themselves.

turns.them: It goes in order: what a cloud is, how a still night makes fog, and how rising air builds a heap. I’ll come back on at the end with a few questions.
Harrow, Walla Walla again. Three questions over the air, like a Bureau examination, only friendlier. First: what kind of night makes fog by dawn?

replies.back: That’s it. A clear sky lets the ground lose its heat, no wind leaves the chilled air lying on the ground, and damp air has its dew point close by.
Backwards. Cloud keeps the ground warm like a blanket, and wind stirs the cold air away. Clear, still and damp is the recipe.
Damp helps, but a cloudy or breezy night after rain stays clear at the ground. You need clear and still as well.

turns.them: Second. The thermometer reads 26 degrees this morning and the dew point is 14. Where will the puffy clouds put their flat bottoms?

replies.back: Twelve degrees of gap at 125 metres a degree. Right on the nose.
That’s one degree’s worth, and you’ve got twelve. Twelve times 125 is 1,500 metres.
Only if there were no gap at all. Twelve degrees at 125 metres a degree puts the base around 1,500 metres.

turns.them: Last one. Small heaps that stay small all afternoon. What do they say?

replies.say: Fair weather. They fade by sunset.
replies.back: Right. Hay can stay out under those.
Not while they stay small. A heap has to grow tall to rain. Small ones are fair weather and fade at sunset.
They say nothing about tomorrow. Small heaps that stay small are fair weather, and fade at sunset.

turns.them: Fog and heaps, blankets and bubbles: the two textures of the whole sky. Next lesson, grey skies.
